replying_to: Replying to Out-of-Distribution Detection and Selective Generation for Conditional Language Models
display_title: Official Review of Paper3086 by Reviewer WGqY

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an out-of-distribution detection mechanism for conditional language models (LMs). The authors investigate settings such as (degrees of) OOD detection for summarisation and translation, and using OOD detection to refrain from generating with the model on-the-fly.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The authors address a timely research question, since LMs popularity is (still) on the rise and LMs are deployed almost as out-of-the-box tools for "language understanding" or "language generation".
- Quite a number of experiments on different aspects of OOD detection. I like the in-depth investigation of the different ideas proposed/studied in the paper.

Weaknesses:
- There are some statements/claims that are either not well developed in the text (leaving to the reader to guess the intention of the authors when saying something) or that seem overeaching/inconsistent. Please refer to my comments for detailed examples of these.
- The paper can be hard to follow at times, and there are a lot of different experiments. Perhaps the authors would have a perceivingly stronger paper by making it less wide and more deep (i.e., cover less different points but go deeper into the points it does cover).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clear enough (nonwithstanding the points mentioned as weaknesses), and includes many interesting experiments. I am not so positive about its reproducibility, since there are no statements about (a plan for open sourcing) code for reproducing the experiments. One point I did not like very much is the fact the authors mention two external baselines at the end of their related work section (the ensemble methods proposed for e.g. machine translation), but do not compare their methods against those baselines. The paper seems to be novel enough, although this is an educated guess by the reviewer (for lack of detailed knowledge about the state-of-the-art).
content.summary_of_the_review:
My recommendation is a borderline accept. The reason for "accept" is the fact the paper is on a timely research topic and that it includes many varied and interesting experiments. The reson for "borderline" is detailed in my comments/questions below.

- The examples of existing works on OOD detection could be greatly improved (2nd paragraph in the introduction). Not sure the cow example is the best one, since it is more an example of "noisy" rather than "out-of-distribution" input. It is also an example in the vision domain, should you not include an example in the (conditional) language modelling domain?

- Page 2, paragraph 1, last sentence ("In Section 4, we show that while model perplexity is a reasonable choice for [performing selective generation with] in-domain examples, combining with our OOD score works much better when the input distribution is shifted") -> Please make it clear that you are talking about selective generation, e.g., I added the text in-between brackets to do that as a suggestion.

- Page 2, section 2: In the first paragraph, it is not clear what is the (practical) relationship between maximum softmax probability (MSP) and perplexity. Please better elaborate your point, the paragraph reads like two more-or-less independent points glued together. A method that comes to mind is the mean over the MSP for a sequential output, for instance.

- Page 3, last paragraph ("MD0(ztest) := MD(ztest; μz0 , Σz0 ) is the MD to a background Gaussian N (μz0 , Σz0 ), fit using a large, broad dataset to approximately represent all domains.") -> Even though I understand the point, in your introduction you mention that, compared to OOD detection in a standard classification problem, performing OOD detection for CLMs have the added difficulty that CLMs have virtually infinite, unbounded output spaces. This idea of "approximately" representing "all domains" goes directly against that point. Please defend why this claim/idea makes sense for OOD detection of CLMs. Is the point made in the introduction not so important afterall?

- Page 4, 2nd paragraph ("While we use the ground-truth outputs to fit N (μw, Σw), we do not have ground-truth in general for the background examples (e.g. C4). We decode outputs from the trained CLMs and use those output embeddings to fit the background output Gaussian, N (μwδ , Σwδ ).") -> This sentence is not clear. Please rephrase. Your model requires input/output for the two tasks, i.e., summarisation and translation. You have C4 for summarisation, and ParaCrawl for translation. Please elaborate that ParaCrawl does not have translation pairs, but paraphrases (right?), and that C4 does not include summaries (to the best of my knowledge). Your descriptions seem incomplete and assume that the reader will make the leap about important points that should be made clear in your manuscript.

- Page 4: "Since we have implicitly defined two classes (...)" -> There was no implicit definition, I would say this definition of the two classes was explicitly made.

- You are using AUROC as your metric, but I would like to see the plots rather than the summary metric (i.e., the actual curves), perhaps in the appendix. As baselines, you are using the perplexity score but not the maximum softmax probability MSP. Could you not use the mean MSP (over the sequence) as a proxy for OOD? Does it consistently underperform compared to using perplexity?

- Page 6: "Though RMD and Binary logits OOD scores both perform well at OOD detection, RMD OOD score is better at distinguishing near-OOD from far-OOD." -> Why does that matter? That is not what models were trained for. If you had trained models (RMD vs. Binary logits) to distinguish between near-OOD and far-OOD, perhaps the outcome would have been different. This split of near- vs. far-OOD is also a bit arbitrary, if you will make it central in your evaluation/discussion (like you do), perhaps it is a good idea to be more principled about it (e.g., using some objective/concrete measure to make one dataset "more OOD than" another). You hint at unigram overlap as a measure of OOD-ness later on, perhaps you should use the "degree of OOD-ness" as the percentage of unigram overlap between the two domains, for example.

- Page 6: "We observed that law has the highest unigram overlap rate (48.8%) and the second highest overall overlap with the in-domain data (Table A.7). This confirms that law is actually not OOD data and explains why no method can detect it." -> If your definition of OOD only depends on unigram overlap, you do not need anything other than computing the unigram overlap between domains to perform OOD detection. I find this a very misleading comment, since the fact a dataset has high unigram overlap with another does not automatically rule out this dataset being OOD. You should include more nuance in these statements.

- Page 7: "Amazon Mechanical Turk workers were asked to evaluate summaries generated by the xsum model on a scale of 1-5 (bad-good) using 100 examples from xsum, cnn dailymail, reddit tifu, and samsum. We collected 3 ratings per example and took the median to reduce inter-rater noise" -> This is a bad strategy to reduce inter-annotator agreement. You are basically hiding the (possible) disagreement by only using the median, whereas in order to reduce the disagreement (and not mask it) you should instead 1) select high-quality annotators, 2) make the annotation guidelines clear including concrete examples of how to annotate difficult cases, 3) include control examples for annotators, etc. Please at least report the variance of the annotators, so the reader knows how noisy they are.

- Page 8, Section 4.4: "To evaluate that, we propose using the Quality vs Abstention Curve (QA), analogous to accuracy versus rejection curve used for selective prediction in the classification." -> Citation missing. You mention Malinin & Gales (2020); Xiao et al. (2020) later, but it is not clear how exactly they relate to QA. If you are the one proposing this measure, please make it clear.

- Page 8, Section 4.4: "For translation, the OOD score is better than perplexity when abstention rate α > 0.5 and worse than perplexity when α < 0.5." -> From Figure 5, the cut-off point looks more like 0.6 or 0.65 rather than 0.5. Is that so?

- Page 9, Section 5, last paragraph: "In this work, we focus on developing scores that can be readily derived from the generative model itself, without much increase in computation." -> You did not compute how much time it takes to run your proposed models compared to the baselines. I find it could be a limitation of your work, especially in light of the existing work using ensembles mentioned in your related work section. You also did not include any such ensembles as your baselines. Why?
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.comment:
> The examples of existing works on OOD detection could be greatly improved (2nd paragraph in the introduction). Not sure the cow example is the best one, since it is more an example of "noisy" rather than "out-of-distribution" input. It is also an example in the vision domain, should you not include an example in the (conditional) language modelling domain?

This is an example taken from the out-of-distribution section from the cited Kevin Murphy book (https://github.com/probml/pml2-book/releases/tag/2022-10-16 , “Chapter 19, beyond the IID assumption, Section 19.2 Distribution Shift”). In this case the shift in the background causes the classifier to fail.

We observed a similar failure mode for a summarization model trained on one news publisher generating poor quality summary for news from a different publisher and added that as a motivating example to the introduction. Section A.14 shows the full examples.

> Page 2, paragraph 1, last sentence ("In Section 4, we show that while model perplexity is a reasonable choice for [performing selective generation with] in-domain examples, combining with our OOD score works much better when the input distribution is shifted") -> Please make it clear that you are talking about selective generation, e.g., I added the text in-between brackets to do that as a suggestion.

Your suggestion is incorporated into the revised version. 

> Page 2, section 2: In the first paragraph, it is not clear what is the (practical) relationship between maximum softmax probability (MSP) and perplexity. Please better elaborate your point, the paragraph reads like two more-or-less independent points glued together. A method that comes to mind is the mean over the MSP for a sequential output, for instance. 

Maximum softmax probability, MSP, is the most commonly used confidence score in classification problems. Perplexity, which is also based on softmax probabilities, is a commonly used loss function for conditional language models. As you suggested, we added a sentence “both are based on softmax probabilities.” for clarification in that paragraph.

We agree that the mean over the MSP for a sequential output can be a baseline to compare. We include it into our revised version (Section A.6), and the results are shown in the table in the [Summary of revision changes](https://openreview.net/forum?id=kJUS5nD0vPB&noteId=REZhCPlNCR). As we can see, the Mean(MSP) performs slightly worse than perplexity, and both perplexity and Mean(MSP) are worse than our proposed methods RMD and Binary logits. 

> Page 3, last paragraph ("MD0(ztest) := MD(ztest; μz0 , Σz0 ) is the MD to a background Gaussian N (μz0 , Σz0 ), fit using a large, broad dataset to approximately represent all domains.") -> Even though I understand the point, in your introduction you mention that, compared to OOD detection in a standard classification problem, performing OOD detection for CLMs have the added difficulty that CLMs have virtually infinite, unbounded output spaces. This idea of "approximately" representing "all domains" goes directly against that point. Please defend why this claim/idea makes sense for OOD detection of CLMs. Is the point made in the introduction not so important afterall?

There are two different concepts: domains and output space. An in-distribution domain here is like a fine-tuning dataset, e.g. g. XSum news articles. For any domain, the output space of language models is infinite. The background model’s purpose is to approximate language in all domains, in contrast to the in-distribution domain. In practice, we approximate this universe with a large dataset comprising many domains → think general pre-training data that are used to train LLMs. There are many possible choices for this, and many LLM works have shown there are many suitable options. For example, [T5 uses C4](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10683), but [GPT-2 collected WebText](https://d4mucfpksywv.cloudfront.net/better-language-models/language-models.pdf), and others have used [The Pile](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.00027). In our [Summary of revision changes](https://openreview.net/forum?id=kJUS5nD0vPB&noteId=REZhCPlNCR) we showed that using C4 sentences or Paracrawl for the translation task works about the same.

We do not assume we have access for near-OOD and far-OOD data for training. We only used those datasets for evaluation. What we meant there is near-OOD and far-OOD datasets have different distribution under RMD, but they overlap significantly under Binary logits, as shown in Figure 3.

It is clear to see that cnn_dailymail and newsroom have significantly higher similarity with the in-domain xsum data than other three datasets. We agree with you that a high unigram overlap does not automatically rule out this dataset being OOD. We do not claim that n-gram overlap is the criterion for OOD. We have made changes in the revision to clarify this point.

We have iterated several times on our MTurk template/worker selection in multiple projects and have found the setup to be highly reproducible. We found our stringent worker selection criteria (Masters located in the US with greater than 95% HITApproval Rate, with at least 1000 HITs approved) to work well. 

Regarding use of median we found the median and mean to be almost identical. We added standard deviation among human raters in Table A.1(a). More specifically, we compute the standard deviation among the 3 raters for each given summary, and report the average across all rated summaries. As shown in the table, the standard deviation is generally less than 0.2 which is about the 1 unit of difference in our original unnormalized rating scale. content.title: (response part 4)
content.comment:
> Page 9, Section 5, last paragraph: "In this work, we focus on developing scores that can be readily derived from the generative model itself, without much increase in computation." -> You did not compute how much time it takes to run your proposed models compared to the baselines. I find it could be a limitation of your work, especially in light of the existing work using ensembles mentioned in your related work section. You also did not include any such ensembles as your baselines. Why?

Thanks for the insightful comments. In the revised paper, we added multiple baselines in Section A.6 including an ensemble method based on MC dropout [3, 4] which aggregates perplexity scores from multiple times of decoding. Ensemble-based score outperforms the perplexity score on OOD detection, but note that the inference time for ensemble-based methods is N times of that for the single model based score. Please find the full table with all the baselines and the method description in [Summary of revision changes](https://openreview.net/forum?id=kJUS5nD0vPB&noteId=REZhCPlNCR) at the top.

[3] Malinin, Andrey, et al. "Shifts: A dataset of real distributional shift across multiple large-scale tasks." arXiv preprint arXiv:2107.07455 (2021).

[4] Xiao, Tim Z., Aidan N. Gomez, and Yarin Gal. "Wat zei je? detecting out-of-distribution translations with variational transformers." arXiv preprint arXiv:2006.08344 (2020).

We also include an analysis of the time complexity required of each method at inference. More specifically, assume that the time complexity for obtaining encoder and decoder representations takes O(E) and O(D), respectively, computing RMD score takes O(R), and we run MC dropout for N times. We also assume O(R) << O(E), O(D): in our experiments, computing RMD on CPU takes only .0015 seconds on CPU per sample. As shown in the table, RMD (output) has the same complexity as perplexity with O(E + D), RMD (input) with O(E), and all three require less computation than MC dropout. 
|Method|Inference time complexity|
|:----|:----|
|ppx|O(E + D)|
|MC dropout|O(N(E + D))|
|RMD (input)|O(E)|
|RMD (output)|O(E + D)|

Besides inference complexity, we’d like to also point out that our method requires minimal fitting. In our case, fitting the Gaussian using 10,000 samples takes only 1.01 seconds on CPU. This is in contrast to many other ensemble approaches, or neural network-based methods that require additional models (e.g., QE metrics like COMET-QE).

display_title: Official Review of Paper3086 by Reviewer f7UA

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper addresses the out-of-domain (OOD) detection for conditional generation tasks. It proposes an OOD score, which is based on the Mahalanobis Distance (MD) to the input and output embeddings of the language model. The MD-based OOD score is computed in relative to a background Gaussian model. Furthermore, the combined OOD score and perplexity correlates well with generation quality, and can be used for selective generation and early rejection based on OOD score. The proposed approaches are validated on summarization and translation tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
(1)	It addresses an interesting OOD problem for conditional generation, where OOD errors can get easily accumulated via auto-regressive generation.
(2)	It proposes an effective OOD score. The score is based on the MD to the input and output embeddings of the language model. Relative MD is used to measure the inference time deviation from training data and a background distribution model.
(3)	The OOD score in combination with perplexity provides a good metric for selective generation of near-domain samples with quality control. It correlates well with generation quality. It is simple to deploy to address the domain shift issue at inference time.
(4)	Experiments and results are well-explained. Analysis is comprehensive. The analysis of the correlation of perplexity and generation quality with OOD score changes is insightful.

Weaknesses:
(1)	Novelty is limited as MD-based OOD metrics have been widely studied and used, though this paper used it in a different setting (non-classification). 
(2)	It is not compared with other common OOD detection strategies, such as threshold based, energy based, contrastive based approaches.
(3)	It’s not clear how the proposed method generalizes to other tasks and model structures.
(4)	It is unclear why the embeddings from the final layers are chosen.
(5)	It is unclear how the background data is selected, and how well the background Gaussian is expected to generalize. It seems fitting the background Gaussian is nontrivial and the proposed method is not as light-weight as it claimed to be. More importantly, what if we know nothing about the OOD? It seems the background Gaussian would fail to work when there is no good definition of background data.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity is good. Experiments are well-explained. Analysis is comprehensive. However, there is too much important material in the Appendix. Would suggest to improve the paper structure and format.

Novelty is limited. It addresses an interesting OOD problem in conditional generation. The proposed approaches are effective. However, MD-based OOD metrics have been extensively studied and used.

Reproducibility is limited. The OOD score fitting and computation are nontrivial. Though the experiment settings and results are thoroughly explained, it is relatively challenging to reproduce all of them due to lack of necessary implementation details.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The problem is interesting, the proposed approach is effective, and experiments and analysis are comprehensive.
Novelty is a bit limited, lack of comparison with other common OOD approaches, and the generalization of the proposed approach is questionable.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

display_title: Thank you for the valuable feedback! Please find our point-to-point response below. (part 1)

content.title: Thank you for the valuable feedback! Please find our point-to-point response below. (part 1)
content.comment:
> “Novelty is limited as MD-based OOD metrics have been widely studied and used, though this paper used it in a different setting (non-classification).”

It is true that MD based OOD methods have been studied, but they were only extensively studied in classification models previously. 

We extend the collection of representative OOD methods previously proposed in classification problems to the CLMs, including the output softmax probability based score (perplexity, MSP, energy score, ensemble scores), and the embedding based scores (MD, RMD, and Binary classifier and KNN-based method), and study their performance in this new setting. We also compared commonly used domain specific scores (NLI, COMET, Prism) which have not been systematically studied for their OOD detection performance. 

OOD detection is just one of the contributions in this work. The other main focus is to predict the output quality using OOD scores and evaluate for selective generation. We showed that in the case of distributional shift, softmax prob based score (perplexity) and OOD scores are complementary in predicting the output quality. Combining the two gives better performance not only than single scores, but also than the neural network-based quality estimation scores (NLI, COMET, and Prism) which are trained on annotated human evaluation data.

> “It is not compared with other common OOD detection strategies, such as threshold based, energy based, contrastive based approaches. “

We focus on developing OOD detection methods for conditional language models (CLMs), instead of the classic well studied classification models. 

In the submitted version, we choose a few representative methods, but agree that other OOD detection methods developed for classification models have potential to be extended to CLMs. So we added a few more baselines in this revision. Those new baseline methods and results are described in [Summary of revision changes](https://openreview.net/forum?id=kJUS5nD0vPB&noteId=REZhCPlNCR).

For contrastive based approaches, as far as we know, those methods are designed for classification problems [6,7] and is unclear how to extend those to conditional language models. Also those methods require substantial modification of the model training using contrastive loss. In this study we hope to develop a lightweight and post-hoc OOD detection method for a given trained conditional language model. We do believe that contrastive learning has the potential to improve OOD detection in conditional language models. We leave it for future research.   

[6] Winkens, Jim, et al. "Contrastive training for improved out-of-distribution detection." arXiv preprint arXiv:2007.05566 (2020).

[7] Zhou, Wenxuan, Fangyu Liu, and Muhao Chen. "Contrastive out-of-distribution detection for pretrained transformers." arXiv preprint arXiv:2104.08812 (2021).

content.comment:
> “It is unclear how the background data is selected, and how well the background Gaussian is expected to generalize. It seems fitting the background Gaussian is nontrivial and the proposed method is not as light-weight as it claimed to be. More importantly, what if we know nothing about the OOD? It seems the background Gaussian would fail to work when there is no good definition of background data.”

The fitting of the background Gaussian follows the same method as the fitting of the foreground in-domain Gaussian. The only two parameters that need to be fitted are the mean $\mu=\frac{1}{n} \sum z_i$, and the covariance matrix $\Sigma^2 = \frac{1}{n} \sum (z_i - \mu)^2$. The steps are clearly shown in Algorithms 1 and 2.  Our proposed method has no hyperparmaters and no extra models (like NLI, COMET and Prism baselines), so there is no need for extra training or finetuning. The background data does not need to have annotated summaries or translation. We simply feed the samples in the background data to the same trained model (Pegasus or T5 model) and extract the last layer embeddings. 

Our principle for choosing the background data is to make it as general as possible. For summarization we use the C4 dataset, which contains a large amount of web crawl documents, to represent a broad range of topics. Similarly for translation, we use ParaCrawl dataset, which is also a large web crawl of sentences, because our translation model is a sentence to sentence model, unlike the summarization model that takes the document as the input. From both studies, we found the two background datasets worked well, and there was no need for further tuning on the background data. 

To further explore the effect of the background data on the performance, we split C4 documents into sentences and use that as the background data to compute the scores, and compare that with using ParaCrawl. The OOD detection performance using C4 sentences is very similar to that using ParaCrawl, as shown in the table provided in [Summary of revision changes](https://openreview.net/forum?id=kJUS5nD0vPB&noteId=REZhCPlNCR). For example, ParaCrawl-based input OOD score has slightly better performance on medial, Koran, IT datasets, while C4 based input score is slightly better at the other datasets. Both are significantly better than the baseline methods, and both give the same ranking of datasets on their OOD-ness, so our conclusion remains. Those results verify that our method is robust to the choice of background data. 

> “It’s not clear how the proposed method generalizes to other tasks and model structures.“

We showed that the proposed methods work for (1) two tasks, summarization and translation, (2) two different models, Pegasus and T5 model. Pegasus is a pretrained and finetuned model, and the T5 translation model is trained from scratch. Transformer-based models [7] have become dominant in conditional language models. 

[7] Vaswani, Ashish, et al. "Attention is all you need." Advances in neural information processing systems 30 (2017).

> “It is unclear why the embeddings from the final layers are chosen.” 

We chose embeddings from final layers because the last layer embedding is what the decoder sees. It gives the highest level of representation. 

In theory, one could compute distances using embeddings from middle layers, but that'd increase the compute and memory. One can also develop a weighted average version of our proposed distances using different layers, but that requires to have validation data to tune the weights. We will pursue this in the future.

> “Clarity is good. Experiments are well-explained. Analysis is comprehensive. However, there is too much important material in the Appendix. Would suggest to improve the paper structure and format.”

Thank you for your suggestion. Due to the page limit, we wanted to present the most interesting ideas and results in the main text and erred on including more in the Appendix for completeness. 

> “Reproducibility is limited. The OOD score fitting and computation are nontrivial. Though the experiment settings and results are thoroughly explained, it is relatively challenging to reproduce all of them due to lack of necessary implementation details.”

Our proposed OOD score is simple to compute. It does not contain any hyperparameters so no need for tuning. In addition, we provided Algorithms 1 and 2 in the appendix. 

The datasets we used are those ones commonly used in the research field, and are all publicly available. 

We uploaded a supplementary file containing an ipython notebook with code demonstrating the method. We will release the human eval data along with the camera ready version.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
Conditional language models often perform poorly on out-of-domain (OOD) data. This might be a reason why they shouldn't be tasked with generating anything for OOD examples at all: generations might be of poor quality and even more unpredictable than normal outputs. In order to predict which examples a conditional language model can be safely applied to, the authors propose a score to detect OOD examples. The score they introduce is Mahalanobis distance, either using the input or the output embeddings. They further show that the latter can be combined with perplexity to obtain an even stronger score.

The authors perform two types of experiments (on summarization and translation). First, they show that their score can detect OOD data more reliably than baselines. Second, they show that their score can also indicate low-quality generations.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper has a clear motivation and succeeds at what it's trying to do.
- The experiments are well designed.

Weaknesses:
- Nothing major.

There are a couple of typos.

content.title: Summary of revision changes
content.comment:
Thanks for the valuable, high-quality feedback from all reviewers.

Below is a summary of major changes. We also have reviewer-specific comments as responses to reviews.

1. Added a few more baseline results for out-of-distribution detection:

We want to note that it is not straightforward to extend the classifier-based OOD scores to CLMs especially for input OOD detection. We would like to include as many possible methods as we can to present a comprehensive comparison for different methods. For those methods that rely on classification head derived logits, energy score [1] and MSP [2], we simply consider the output decoding process as a sequence of classification decisions over tokens, and take the average of the corresponding score over the generated output tokens $y_1,...,y_T$ as the output OOD scores.

In the revision, we added a few more baselines as suggested:

- Energy score averaged over the output sequence tokens [1]

- Maximum softmax probability (MSP) averaged over the output sequence tokens [2]

- Ensemble estimation of the output perplexity from multiple Monte-Carlo dropout samples. [3,4] propose to turn on the MC dropout layer at inference time and sample multiple times (N) using different random seeds as a way to approximate Bayesian neural networks. We follow their idea and generate multiple output sequences and use the averaged perplexity as the uncertainty score. Note that the inference time for ensemble-based methods is N times of that for the single model based score.

- KNN-based OOD score. [5] propose to use the distance to the $k$-th nearest neighbor in the training set in the embedding space as an OOD score. There are two hyper-parameters in the KNN-based method, $k$ and $\alpha$. $\alpha$ is the proportion of training data sampled for nearest neighbor calculation, and k refers to the k-th nearest neighbor. We use the optimal $k=1000$ and $\alpha=100$ as suggested by the paper. We also normalize the embedding features since the paper showed the feature normalization is critical for good performance. 

Mean(MSP), energy score, and ensembled perplexity score, are all derived from the logits of the tokens in output sequences, so they are output OOD scores. The KNN-based method can be applied for both input sequence embeddings and output sequence embeddings.

The following table shows the AUROCs for OOD detection for the newly added baselines, as a comparison to our methods. First, the logits based output OOD scores, perplexity, mean(MSP), energy score, even the ensembled perplexity score which costs N times of the inference time, are in general not competitive with our proposed methods RMD and Binary logits. Though the energy score is a bit better than perplexity and mean(MSP), and ensembled score is better than energy score, the performance gap between those methods and our proposed method is still big, especially for the near-OOD datasets. Second, KNN-based methods are not as good as MD and RMD either. Though it is possible that the optimal hyper-parameters suggested by the paper may not be the optimal ones for our problem, searching for the optimal hyper-parameters requires a separate validation set. Our proposed methods have no hyperparameters. We added the results into our revised paper as Section A.6.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
The paper proposes an out-of-distribution detection mechanism for conditional language models (LMs). The authors investigate settings such as (degrees of) OOD detection for summarisation and translation, conditional generation, and using OOD detection to refrain from generating with the model on-the-fly.

Timely research topic though only limited to conditional generation in working with LMs.  Many interesting experiments though reproducibility may be difficult.   OOD detection is well studied in text classification so this is not a major step for LMs.  A lot of good comments from reviewers to be addressed.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: The method is limited in scope (conditional models only) and there are questions about the extent of originality and challenges in reproducibility.
